stories.topicLabel: Mail-in voting uncertainty ahead of midterms
stories.analysis: Coverage of mail-in voting uncertainty ahead of the midterms was largely uniform, spanning only one point across all scored headlines. The most notable framing variation came from NPR, whose two headlines leaned slightly left by foregrounding threats to mail-in voters — phrases like "backup plans amid uncertainty" and "ballot seizures seemed impossible" conveyed a sense of credible danger and invited reader sympathy toward voters navigating those risks. By contrast, the Washington Examiner's neutral status-check framing — "Where does mail-in voting stand?" — treated the topic as a factual policy question without implying urgency or threat. The New York Times similarly stayed neutral with the descriptive phrase "would work," offering a process-oriented account of Trump's mail voting plan. Across all outlets, the shared baseline was informational reporting on mail-in voting logistics; the modest differences were tonal rather than ideological, with NPR's choice of alarming specifics being the clearest departure from otherwise even-handed framing.

stories.topicLabel: Germany's Merz accuses AfD of ethnic cleansing agenda
stories.analysis: The 2.5-point spread here reflects a genuine framing divergence, concentrated mainly at the left end of the spectrum. Vox anchors the far-left position with pointed editorial choices: calling AfD "Nazi-curious" rather than "far-right," and appending "The White House approves" to frame the Trump administration as complicit in extremism — neither phrase appears in any factual reporting elsewhere. Axios adds softer left-coded language, noting that "nostalgia carries a dark past" to draw an implicit parallel between Trump's rhetoric and Germany's history. By contrast, Reuters and the Washington Examiner occupy essentially neutral ground, both using the unadorned verb "accuses" and quoting Merz's "ethnic cleansing" charge without additional editorial coloring. The core diplomatic facts — Merz's accusation, Trump's praise of AfD, the postponed call — appear across outlets, but the ideological temperature is almost entirely a product of how Vox and Axios chose to contextualize those facts.

stories.topicLabel: SEC considers expelling LSU over roster rules
stories.analysis: Coverage of this story was largely uniform, with a bias spread of just 1.5 points across all outlets. The two straight-news headlines from the AP and USA Today used nearly identical neutral framing, describing the SEC's position factually — phrases like "discuss expelling LSU" and "legal battle over Tigers' roster escalates" conveyed the situation without editorializing. The only notable departure was a USA Today opinion column headlined "LSU must take its SEC punishment. Or take a hike," which introduced a more pointed, directive tone through the phrase "take a hike." Importantly, scorers flagged this difference as stylistic rather than ideologically political — the column's framing reflects the conventions of opinion writing rather than a left or right lean. Readers should note that the harder-edged language in that piece is genre-driven, and the underlying factual framing across all three headlines remains substantively consistent.
